title: Seek Me and Live: Let Justice Roll Like a River
summary: Amos sings a funeral lament over Israel as though the nation were already dead, then calls the people to seek the LORD and live rather than seek the shrines of Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. He condemns those who turn justice to wormwood, take bribes, and silence honest witnesses in the city gate. He warns that the Day of the LORD will be darkness, not light, and God declares that he hates Israel's feasts and wants justice to roll on like a river.
story: This chapter stands at the center of the book of Amos. Chapter 4 ended with the summons to prepare to meet God; chapter 5 shows what that meeting will be like, and still holds open the door of mercy with three calls to seek and live. It gathers every major theme of the book: the certainty of judgment, the corruption of the courts, the emptiness of worship without obedience, and the misplaced confidence of a people who assumed God was on their side. The famous words of verse 24 have become one of the Old Testament's best-known lines. The chapter prepares for the woes against the complacent rich in chapter 6 and the visions of judgment in chapters 7 to 9.
historical:
Amos spoke around 760 BC, when the northern kingdom under Jeroboam II was at its height. The lament of verses 1 and 2 would have sounded absurd to his hearers, who had no reason to think the nation was dying. Yet within four decades the Assyrian empire had destroyed Samaria (722 BC) and deported much of the population "beyond Damascus" (verse 27), into Assyrian territory in Mesopotamia and beyond (2 Kings 17:6). Verse 3's picture of a city sending out a thousand soldiers and seeing a hundred return describes the losses of a militia raised from towns and villages.

Bethel and Gilgal were the northern kingdom's main shrines. Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, was associated with Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 21:33; 26:23-25), and northerners evidently made pilgrimages there across the border. The "stone houses" of verse 11 were built of hewn, squared stone, an expensive technique (ashlar masonry) found in royal and elite buildings in Israel at this period, including at Samaria. Sakkuth and Kaiwan (verse 26) are generally understood as names or titles of Mesopotamian astral deities, Kaiwan being associated with the planet Saturn, though their exact identity and the Hebrew text of the verse are debated.
cultural:
In ancient Israelite towns, the city gate was the public square and the courtroom. Its passageway had benches or chambers where elders sat to hear disputes, witness transactions, and give judgment (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-11). When Amos says the powerful "hate the one who reproves in the gate" and "deprive the poor of justice in the gate", he means that the village court, the place where an ordinary person could find a fair hearing, has been bought. The tax of grain in verse 11 probably refers to levies or rents extracted from small farmers by landowners or officials.

A lament (qinah) was a funeral song, sung with a limping rhythm, typically for someone already dead. Wormwood was a plant with a notoriously bitter taste; to turn justice into wormwood is to make what should be sweet and healing into something poisonous. The Pleiades and Orion (verse 8) are the star cluster and constellation still known by those names; the Old Testament mentions them also in Job 9:9 and 38:31 as works of the creator. The "Day of the LORD" was already a popular hope in Israel, a day when God would fight for his people against their enemies.
literary: Many scholars see the chapter's first seventeen verses as a carefully built chiasm, a pattern in which the second half mirrors the first around a center. It opens with lament (verses 1 to 3) and closes with wailing (verses 16 and 17); inside that frame come calls to seek and live (verses 4 to 6 and 14 and 15), charges of corrupted justice (verse 7 and verses 10 to 13), and at the center a hymn to God the creator (verses 8 and 9), ending "the LORD is His name". Verses 18 to 27 then begin a new unit with "Woe", overturning the popular hope in the Day of the LORD, and conclude with God's rejection of festivals and sacrifices. The chapter is full of reversals: those who seek shrines will find exile, those who long for the Day will meet darkness, and those who built stone houses will never live in them.

outline.t: A funeral song for Virgin Israel
Seek Me and live, not Bethel
Justice turned to wormwood, and the maker of the stars
Seek good, hate evil, establish justice
Wailing in the streets and vineyards
The Day of the LORD is darkness
I hate your feasts: let justice roll on

doctrines.note: Three times the chapter says "live": seek the LORD, seek good, hate evil and love good. Repentance means turning to God himself and, at the same time, restoring justice in public life. The "perhaps" of verse 15 keeps it humble; mercy is hoped for, not presumed.

Amos overturns the popular hope that the Day of the LORD would bring victory. God's day of judgment falls first on his own unfaithful people. There is no safe distance from it, as the images of the lion, the bear, and the snake make clear.

God's rejection of Israel's worship (verses 21 to 23) shows that he cannot be honored by ritual that coexists with injustice. His holiness is moral, and worship that ignores what he commands offends rather than pleases him.

Justice and righteousness, the central demands of verse 24, sum up the purpose of Israel's law: fair courts, protection for the weak, honest dealing. Amos calls not for a new law but for the old one to be lived.

words.note: Darash, to seek. It can mean to consult a shrine or oracle, which is exactly what Israel was doing at Bethel and Gilgal. Amos redirects the word: "Seek Me and live", and "Seek the LORD and live". What Israel needs is not religious activity but God himself.

Mishpat, justice. It covers the whole work of judging rightly: fair verdicts, protection of the vulnerable, and the right ordering of relationships in society. Amos accuses Israel of turning it into wormwood and calls for it to roll on like a river.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. In the Old Testament it means faithfulness to the obligations of relationship, with God and with neighbors. Paired with mishpat, it describes a community where people keep faith with each other. Israel has cast it to the ground.

Qinah, a lament or funeral dirge. Amos takes up a qinah over Israel while the nation is still prosperous, a shocking act that treats its death as certain. The dirge often used a distinctive uneven rhythm, three beats followed by two.

christ: Verse 24 has echoed through Christian history as a summons to let faith show itself in public justice. Jesus stood in the same prophetic line when he rebuked those who tithed garden herbs but neglected "the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness" (Matthew 23:23), and when he quoted Hosea's "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13). Stephen quoted verses 25 to 27, following the Greek translation of the Old Testament, in his speech before the council, to show that Israel's history had long been marked by idolatry (Acts 7:42-43). The chapter's warning about the Day of the LORD also prepares for the New Testament's teaching that the day of the Lord will come like a thief (1 Thessalonians 5:2), and that the only safe place on that day is in Christ, who bore judgment for his people. These connections are partly direct quotation and partly shared conviction.

hard.q: Does Amos reject sacrifice and worship altogether?
hard.a: Verses 21 to 25 sound as if God rejects Israel's entire worship system, and verse 25 asks whether Israel brought sacrifices during the forty years in the wilderness. Some scholars have concluded that Amos opposed sacrificial worship in principle, or that he knew a tradition in which sacrifice played little role in the wilderness period. Most interpreters read the passage differently. They note that Amos addresses a specific people whose worship coexisted with bribery and oppression, and that similar prophetic words (Isaiah 1:11-17; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8) reject worship without obedience rather than worship as such. On this reading, verse 25's question points out that Israel's relationship with God in the wilderness rested on more than offerings, or that even then Israel mixed its worship with idolatry (verse 26). What the passage makes unmistakable is that God does not accept worship as a substitute for justice. The debate is about how far the rejection extends, not about that central point.

questions: God says, "Seek Me and live", and warns against seeking shrines instead. What religious activities can take the place of seeking God himself?
The city gate was where ordinary people found justice. Where in your community do people with little power look for a fair hearing, and what would it mean to establish justice there?
Israel longed for the Day of the LORD, assuming it would be good news for them. What assumptions about God's favor might you need to examine?
